notes.b: Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 on the hygiene of foodstuffs is an EU regulation, which applies directly in every member state. Ireland gives effect to it through national regulations.
points: The European Communities (Hygiene of Foodstuffs) Regulations 2006, amended in 2009 and 2010, give effect to Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 in Ireland.
The Regulations set hygiene standards for food premises.
They require food businesses to operate a food safety system based on HACCP.
They require staff to be trained in hygiene and to follow hygiene procedures.
They require food premises to be registered.
They permit the closure of premises, and the destruction of food, where public health is immediately threatened.

notes.b: Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011 on the provision of food information to consumers is given effect in Ireland by the European Union (Provision of Food Information to Consumers) Regulations 2014.
points: A label must give the name of the food and a list of ingredients in descending order of weight at the time of manufacture.
Fourteen named allergens must be emphasised wherever they appear in the list of ingredients.
A label must give the net quantity of the food and the storage conditions needed to keep it safe.
A use-by date must appear on highly perishable food, after which the food must not be eaten.
A best-before date shows the date until which the food keeps its quality.
A label must give the name and address of the food business operator.
A nutrition declaration gives the energy value, fat, saturates, carbohydrate, sugars, protein and salt of the food.
Labelling must not mislead the consumer about the nature, origin or characteristics of the food.

notes.h: General framework of food law (Higher Level only)
points: The Food Safety Authority of Ireland Act 1998 provides the Irish legal framework for food safety and for the functions of the FSAI.
Regulation (EC) No 178/2002, known as general food law, sets the general principles and requirements of food law across the EU.
Under general food law, food that is unsafe must not be placed on the market.
Food businesses must be able to trace food one step back to their supplier and one step forward to their customers.
General food law set up the European Food Safety Authority and the Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed.
Risk analysis under general food law has three parts: risk assessment, risk management and risk communication.
Regulation (EU) 2017/625 sets out the rules for official controls, which check that food businesses comply with food law at every stage of the food chain.
It is given effect in Ireland by the European Union (Official Controls in Relation to Food Legislation) Regulations 2020.
Official controls include inspection, sampling, analysis and audit.
Official controls are carried out by competent authorities, which in Ireland are the FSAI and the official agencies it contracts.
Official controls are carried out on a risk basis, so that higher-risk businesses are checked more often.
Inspectors can take samples of food for testing as part of an official control.

keyTerms.definition: A binding European law that applies directly in every member state without needing national legislation.
The process by which a national law, such as an Irish statutory instrument, puts an EU regulation into force in Ireland.
Any person or company responsible for a food business, such as a shop, caterer or manufacturer, who must ensure that food is safe.
A body designated by law to carry out official controls and enforce food law.
An inspection, sampling, analysis or audit carried out by a competent authority to check compliance with food law.
The ability to track food one step back to its supplier and one step forward to its customers.
The date on highly perishable food after which it must not be eaten.
The date until which food keeps its quality, after which it may be less palatable but may still be safe to eat.
The mandatory list of the energy and main nutrients in a packaged food, given on its label.
Regulation (EC) No 178/2002, which sets the general principles and requirements of food law in the EU.

questions.prompt: Identify two items of information that must appear on the label of a packaged food, and explain how each one protects the consumer.
questions.model: Ingredients list in descending order of weight, with named allergens emphasised: a consumer with an allergy can avoid foods that would cause a reaction. Use-by or best-before date: the consumer knows whether highly perishable food is still safe to eat, or whether quality has declined. Nutrition declaration of energy and nutrients: the consumer can make informed choices. Name and address of the food business operator: the consumer knows who is responsible for the food. Labelling must not mislead, so the consumer receives accurate information about the food.

questions.prompt: Describe the protection that food legislation gives the consumer, referring to the European Communities (Hygiene of Foodstuffs) Regulations 2006 and to Regulation (EC) No 178/2002.
questions.model: Hygiene of Foodstuffs Regulations 2006, which give effect to Regulation (EC) No 852/2004 in Ireland: they set hygiene standards for food premises; require a HACCP-based food safety system and hygiene training for staff; require food premises to be registered; and permit the closure of premises and the destruction of food where public health is immediately threatened. General food law, Regulation (EC) No 178/2002: unsafe food must not be placed on the market; food businesses must trace food one step back and one step forward, so that unsafe food can be withdrawn or recalled quickly; the Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed passes warnings between countries; and risk assessment, risk management and risk communication guide decisions that protect public health.
